newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil stands firm over Americas free trade. [CORRECTED 23:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Brazil stands firm over Americas free trade. [CORRECTED 23:55 GMT]

text.p: Brazil on Monday sent a clear message to Washington that the United States would have to give as well as take in free trade talks set to take place in the industrial city of Belo Horizonte this week.

"Regional integration depends a lot more on the capacity of countries to the north to open up their markets ... than on our disposition in the south to integrate (our economies)," said Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
"Integration in today's world is no longer done through simple adhesion but through negotiation," he said in Brasilia.

Cardoso spoke two days before government ministers from Tierra del Fuego to the Bering Strait were due to gather in Belo Horizonte for the third ministerial meeting of the 34 Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) signatory countries.
The talks were expected to be the battleground for a test of wills between the United States and South America's Mercosur trade bloc, led by Brazil but also grouping Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.

Launched at the Miami summit in 1994, the FTAA foresees the setting up of a free trade area of one billion potential consumers by the year 2005 that would rival the economic muscle of the European Union.
Belo Horizonte was supposed to determine the timetable and nature of formal free trade negotiations.
But the meeting may come unstuck because of disagreement between Brazil, speaking for Mercosur, and Washington.

Brazil is keen to strengthen Mercosur and less keen to see tariff cuts feed a dramatically expanding trade gap -- $5.5 billion in 1996 and seen reaching up to $12 billion this year. It wants to leave tariff talks until last.
Brazil is also seeking assurances from Washington that free trade will apply to all sectors, including agriculture, where Brazilian products face a series of non-tariff barriers.
The United States, on the other hand, is determined to push through free trade as fast as possible.
U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley, in Rio de Janeiro at the start of a South American tour, also stood his ground.
"In order to reach the goal of 2005, we have to deal with the difficult issues, like market access, upfront," he said.

The United States won a boost on Monday with the publication of an interview with Chilean Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat, who told Brazil's O Globo newspaper that Santiago considered free trade across the Americas a higher priority than Mercosur.

"We consider a priority the establishment of a large area of free trade in the Americas, which is the higher objective of the FTAA," said Aninat, whose country has an associate agreement with Mercosur.
The Belo Horizonte FTAA meeting was due to begin on Tuesday with a businessmen's forum, followed on Thursday and Friday by the ministerial negotiations.
